sections.normalized_html:
Given a natural number [MATH: n,] Euler's totient function [MATH: \phi(n)] returns the total number of positive integers that are less than [MATH: n] and are coprime to [MATH: n.]

First, notice that [MATH: 47] is a prime number. This means that all positive integers that are less than [MATH: 47] are coprime to [MATH: 47.] That is to say, the numbers [MATH: 1,2,3, \ldots, 46] are all coprime to [MATH: 47.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \phi(47) = 47-1 = 46.]

In general, [MATH: \phi(p) = p-1,] where [MATH: p] is prime.

Content:
There is a nice rule that allows us to easily calculate Euler's totient function when the argument is a prime number raised to a positive integer power.

Content:
> If [MATH: p] is a prime and [MATH: k] is a positive integer, then
> [MATH: \phi \left(p^k\right)=p^k-p^{k-1}.]

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: \phi(2^7).] First, notice that [MATH: 2^7] is the seventh power ([MATH: k=7]) of the prime number [MATH: p=2.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: ϕ(2^{7})|= p^{k} − p^{k − 1}; = 2^{7} − 2^{7 − 1}; = 128 − 64; = 64.]

Content:
To see why this rule works, recall that [MATH: \phi(p^k)] returns the number of positive integers less than [MATH: p^k] that are coprime to [MATH: p^k.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: p] is a prime number, we have that

Content:
- the only possible values of [MATH: \mathrm{gcd}\left(m, p^k\right)] are [MATH: 1,p, p^2, \ldots, p^{k},] and
- [MATH: \mathrm{gcd}\left(m, p^k\right)\neq 1] only if [MATH: m] is a multiple of [MATH: p,] i.e.,
[MATH: m= p, \: 2p, \: \ldots, \: p^{k-1}p.]

Content:
So, since there are [MATH: p^{k-1}] multiples of [MATH: p] that are less than or equal to [MATH: p^k,] there must be [MATH: p^k-p^{k-1}] numbers less than [MATH: p^k] that are coprime to [MATH: p^k.] Therefore, [MATH: \phi \left(p^k\right)=p^k-p^{k-1}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
Given a natural number [MATH: n,] Euler's totient function [MATH: \phi(n)] returns the total number of positive integers that are less than [MATH: n] and are coprime to [MATH: n.]

Moreover, if [MATH: n=p^k,] where [MATH: k\geq 1] is a natural number and [MATH: p] is prime, then

[MATH: \phi(n) = \phi(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1}.]

Notice that [MATH: 32 = 2^5] is the fifth power ([MATH: k=5]) of the prime number [MATH: p=2.] Therefore,

[MATH: ϕ(2^{5})|= p^{k} − p^{k − 1}; = 2^{5} − 2^{5 − 1}; = 32 − 16; = 16.]

It can be shown that Euler's totient function is a multiplicative function, meaning that if two positive integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are coprime, then [MATH: \phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n).]

Content:
This property can be used to simplify many calculations.

Content:
For example, let's use the property to calculate [MATH: \phi(51).] First, notice that

Content:
Since [MATH: 3] and [MATH: 17] are prime numbers, we have

sections.normalized_html:
Given a natural number [MATH: n,] Euler's totient function [MATH: \phi(n)] returns the total number of positive integers that are less than [MATH: n] and are coprime to [MATH: n.]

Recall that Euler's totient function is a multiplicative function, meaning that if two positive integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are coprime, then [MATH: \phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n).]

First, notice that

[MATH: 210 = 5\cdot 6 \cdot 7.]

  • Since [MATH: 5] and [MATH: 7] are distinct prime numbers, we have [MATH: ϕ(5)|= 5 − 1 = 4,; ϕ(7)|= 7 − 1 = 6.]

  • To compute [MATH: \phi(6),] let's write down all positive integers that are less than [MATH: 6] and cancel out the numbers that are not coprime to [MATH: 6\mathbin{:}] [MATH: \require{cancel} 1, \: \bcancel{2}, \: \bcancel{3}, \bcancel{4},\: 5] So, [MATH: \phi(6) = 2.]

Finally, since [MATH: \phi] is multiplicative and [MATH: \text{gcd}(5,6,7)=1,] we obtain

[MATH: ϕ(210)|= ϕ(5) ⋅ ϕ(6) ⋅ ϕ(7); = 4 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 6; = 48.]

Content:

Content:

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Given a natural number [MATH: n,] Euler's totient function [MATH: \phi(n)] returns the number of positive integers that are less than [MATH: n] and are coprime to [MATH: n.] Here, [MATH: \phi] is the Greek letter phi.

Content:
To illustrate, let's calculate [MATH: \phi(12).] Since [MATH: 12] is a small number, we can first write down all positive integers that are less than [MATH: 12,] and then remove any numbers that are not coprime to [MATH: 12\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: \require{cancel}
1, \: \bcancel{2}, \: \bcancel{3}, \: \bcancel{4}, \: {5}, \: \bcancel{6}, \: {7}, \: \bcancel{8}, \: \bcancel{9}, \: \bcancel{10}, 11]

Content:
We end up with only [MATH: 4] positive integers that are less than [MATH: 12] and are coprime to [MATH: 12.] These numbers are [MATH: 1,5,7,] and [MATH: 11.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: \phi(12) = 4.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Evaluating Euler's Totient Function in the Simplest Cases

Example Prompt:
What is the value of [MATH: \phi(47),] where [MATH: \phi] is Euler's totient function?

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
Given a natural number [MATH: n,] Euler's totient function [MATH: \phi(n)] returns the total number of positive integers that are less than [MATH: n] and are coprime to [MATH: n.]

First, notice that [MATH: 47] is a prime number. This means that all positive integers that are less than [MATH: 47] are coprime to [MATH: 47.] That is to say, the numbers [MATH: 1,2,3, \ldots, 46] are all coprime to [MATH: 47.]

Therefore,

[MATH: \phi(47) = 47-1 = 46.]

In general, [MATH: \phi(p) = p-1,] where [MATH: p] is prime.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Euler's Totient Function When the Argument is a Power of a Prime

Content:
There is a nice rule that allows us to easily calculate Euler's totient function when the argument is a prime number raised to a positive integer power.

Content:
> If [MATH: p] is a prime and [MATH: k] is a positive integer, then
> [MATH: \phi \left(p^k\right)=p^k-p^{k-1}.]

Content:
For example, suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: \phi(2^7).] First, notice that [MATH: 2^7] is the seventh power ([MATH: k=7]) of the prime number [MATH: p=2.] Therefore,

Content:
[MATH: ϕ(2^{7})|= p^{k} − p^{k − 1}; = 2^{7} − 2^{7 − 1}; = 128 − 64; = 64.]

Content:
To see why this rule works, recall that [MATH: \phi(p^k)] returns the number of positive integers less than [MATH: p^k] that are coprime to [MATH: p^k.]

Content:
Now, since [MATH: p] is a prime number, we have that

Content:
- the only possible values of [MATH: \mathrm{gcd}\left(m, p^k\right)] are [MATH: 1,p, p^2, \ldots, p^{k},] and
- [MATH: \mathrm{gcd}\left(m, p^k\right)\neq 1] only if [MATH: m] is a multiple of [MATH: p,] i.e.,
[MATH: m= p, \: 2p, \: \ldots, \: p^{k-1}p.]

Content:
So, since there are [MATH: p^{k-1}] multiples of [MATH: p] that are less than or equal to [MATH: p^k,] there must be [MATH: p^k-p^{k-1}] numbers less than [MATH: p^k] that are coprime to [MATH: p^k.] Therefore, [MATH: \phi \left(p^k\right)=p^k-p^{k-1}.]

Moreover, if [MATH: n=p^k,] where [MATH: k\geq 1] is a natural number and [MATH: p] is prime, then

[MATH: \phi(n) = \phi(p^k) = p^k - p^{k-1}.]

Notice that [MATH: 32 = 2^5] is the fifth power ([MATH: k=5]) of the prime number [MATH: p=2.] Therefore,

[MATH: ϕ(2^{5})|= p^{k} − p^{k − 1}; = 2^{5} − 2^{5 − 1}; = 32 − 16; = 16.]

Item 9 — Tutorial: The Multiplicativity of Euler's Totient Function

Content:
It can be shown that Euler's totient function is a multiplicative function, meaning that if two positive integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: n] are coprime, then [MATH: \phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n).]

Content:
This property can be used to simplify many calculations.

Content:
For example, let's use the property to calculate [MATH: \phi(51).] First, notice that

Content:
[MATH: 51 = 3 \cdot 17.]

Content:
Since [MATH: 3] and [MATH: 17] are prime numbers, we have

Content:
[MATH: ϕ(3)|= 3 − 1 = 2,; ϕ(17)|= 17 − 1 = 16.]

Content:
Then, using that [MATH: \phi] is multiplicative and [MATH: \text{gcd}(3,17)=1,] we obtain

Content:
[MATH: ϕ(51)|= ϕ(3) ⋅ ϕ(17); = 2 ⋅ 16; = 32.]

[MATH: \phi(mn) = \phi(m)\phi(n).]

[MATH: 210 = 5\cdot 6 \cdot 7.]

[MATH: ϕ(210)|= ϕ(5) ⋅ ϕ(6) ⋅ ϕ(7); = 4 ⋅ 2 ⋅ 6; = 48.]
